candidateRows: The earliest Christian literature presents Jesus only through revelation and does not clearly locate him in recent earthly history.
This is the first of Carrier's three stated pillars and directly supports the revelatory-Christ alternative in the debate motion.
Carrier argues from Pauline descriptions and omissions that apostles encountered Jesus by revelation rather than as disciples of a recently deceased teacher.
Jesus first becomes an earthly historical figure in mythologically composed Gospels that lack independent corroboration.
The argument addresses the principal narrative evidence for historicity by claiming it derives from a single developing mythic tradition.
Carrier maintains that an unknown Gospel author historicized Jesus through mythical composition and that later accounts merely rewrote this source without independent confirmation.
Common attempts to infer Jesus's historicity from Gospel details fail because those details first appear in unsourced myth and may conflict with Paul.
This move anticipates and rejects major historicist inferences involving Nazareth, disciples, earthly execution, kinship, and human descent.
Carrier argues that supposedly historical biographical details are unattested or contradicted in Paul and were introduced by later Gospel mythology.
Paul's incarnate Jesus was most plausibly killed by Satanic powers in the firmament rather than by earthly authorities.
The move supplies a positive celestial-crucifixion model needed to explain how Carrier's revelatory Jesus could acquire flesh, die, and be resurrected.
MacDonald's request for a concrete account of where Paul's revelatory Jesus became incarnate and was killed.
Carrier proposes a once-for-all heavenly incarnation and killing by demonic agents, comparing the model with Osiris traditions and an early layer of Ascension of Isaiah.
Later noncanonical and so-called Gnostic texts cannot establish the earliest Christian view because they are derivative or too late.
The response defines which sources Carrier regards as chronologically probative and blocks an attempted test of his thesis using later Christian literature.
MacDonald's question whether Christian Gnostic texts provide support for Carrier's proposed revelatory Jesus.
Carrier rejects the evidentiary usefulness of Gnostic materials, contending that no surviving alternative Gospel is demonstrably earlier than the canonical tradition.
Despite early mythologizing and editorial distortion, the Gospels preserve a historical Jewish teacher from first-century Roman Palestine.
This is an explicit historical-Jesus thesis that directly answers the motion while conceding extensive mythmaking around the underlying person.
Carrier's opening contention that Jesus began as a revelatory being and was placed into earthly history only by mythic Gospels.
MacDonald adopts the core of Hoffman's position that literary complexity and mythic accretion do not erase the Gospels' underlying historical coordinates and teachings.
Hoffman's attack neither addressed Carrier's later historicity case nor showed that realistic biographical details distinguish Jesus from mythical figures.
The reply challenges both the relevance of the cited polemic and its substantive inference from realistic Gospel details to a historical Jesus.
MacDonald's adopted Hoffman critique that Gospel realism preserves a historical Jesus and renders mythicism methodologically implausible.
Carrier notes that Hoffman wrote before Carrier's principal book, denies reliance on conspiracy, and argues that named relatives and obscure origins also occur in acknowledged myths.
Carrier's recent work is substantially more successful at dismantling historical reconstructions than at providing a constructive alternative.
This methodological challenge motivates MacDonald's ensuing positive reconstruction and identifies a claimed explanatory weakness in Carrier's case.
Carrier's rebuttal of Hoffman's criticism and his broader mythicist reconstruction of Christian origins.
MacDonald characterizes Carrier's approach as powerfully destructive but constructively inadequate, then transitions to his own historical explanation for the evidence.
The independent and early Q tradition portrays Jesus as a mortal Jewish law reformer modeled on historical prophets, not as a preexistent revelatory savior.
The move offers MacDonald's principal positive early-source case for a historical teacher whose concern was compassionate reform of Jewish law.
Carrier's claim that the earliest evidence knows only a revelatory Jesus and that earthly biography begins in mythological Gospel composition.
MacDonald dates Q near the Pauline letters and argues that its mortal Jesus resembles Moses and the prophets, opposes Pharisaic burdens, and lacks a preexistent salvation role.
Paul's theology requires only a mortal Jesus crucified over a dispute about Jewish law, even though Paul subsequently mythologizes his resurrection.
The claim directly counters the inference that Paul's limited biographical detail and resurrection theology imply an originally celestial rather than historical Jesus.
Carrier's reliance on Paul's silence and revelatory Christology as evidence against a historical Jesus.
After arguing that Q presents Jesus as a mortal reformer of Jewish law, MacDonald extends the same historical-law framework to Paul's theology.
Josephus's account of James, identified through Jesus called Christ, supplies external evidence for Jesus and coheres with a movement divided over Jewish law.
This is a direct attempt to provide independent historical attestation for Jesus, addressing a decisive evidentiary requirement in the historicity dispute.
Carrier's position that no external evidence securely attests a historical Jesus.
MacDonald reads Josephus's James passage as presupposing prior knowledge of Jesus and links the execution controversy to Q and Pauline disputes over Mosaic law.
Mark is too thoroughly mythologized to preserve much independent history, yet its epic comparison makes best sense as transforming a mortal Jewish teacher into a superior hero.
The move concedes extensive literary invention while arguing that such invention presupposes the historical mortal whom Mark elevates, preserving the pro side's core inference.
Carrier's use of Mark's extensive literary construction and mythologization to undermine its historical value.
MacDonald accepts that Mark and later gospels are heavily dependent on mythic narrative but argues that Mark elevates a mortal Galilean above epic heroes.
First John and Papias preserve early claims of eyewitness contact and named disciples, so the Johannine tradition offers evidence that a mythologized Jesus nevertheless existed.
The argument offers purported early personal and transmitted testimony for Jesus, directly bearing on whether Christianity began without a historical earthly founder.
Carrier's skeptical treatment of later Christian traditions as insufficient evidence for an earthly Jesus.
MacDonald invokes First John's sensory-witness language and Papias's preference for living voices, while conceding that the Fourth Gospel mythologizes Jesus.
Matthew's Mosaic Jesus can be explained as reifying communal, scriptural, or revelatory teachings, so Mosaic mythologization does not discriminate between historicity and mythicism.
The move attacks MacDonald's inference from a Jewish-teacher substrate by presenting an alternative causal account that predicts the same Mosaic literary evidence without a historical Jesus.
MacDonald's claim that Matthew or Q inherited oral memories of Jesus as an alternative Moses and interpreter of law.
Carrier accepts that Matthew constructs Jesus through Moses but argues that authors could place evolving teachings into an earthly figure without preserving memories of a teacher.
Mark converts Pauline teachings into earthly Jesus stories while omitting Paul's preexistent cosmology, leaving no evidence to distinguish literary reification from memories of a teacher.
This supplies a positive mythicist mechanism for the transition from a revelatory Pauline Christ to an earthly narrative Jesus, closely matching the debate's central alternative.
MacDonald's objection that the reconstructed tradition presents an earthly figure rather than teachings received through revelation.
Carrier argues that Mark strips away Pauline cosmology, turns teachings into ordinary prophetic narrative, and thereby creates evidence compatible with either origin theory.
Overlaps between Paul and reconstructed Q, especially their kingdom-of-God language, indicate shared traditions and make derivation of the gospel tradition from Paul feel forced and unnecessary.
The shared-tradition argument challenges Carrier's Pauline-to-gospel reification model and supports an independent stream of material associated with an earthly Jewish teacher.
Carrier's claim that no surviving evidence distinguishes reified Pauline teachings from genuine memories of an earthly teacher.
MacDonald lists parallel mission, divorce, follower, return, and kingdom traditions, allowing some Pauline influence but favoring shared tradition over wholesale derivation.
Mythologization alone does not imply nonexistence, but its extraordinary extent requires independent evidence, and Josephus's James passage can be explained without a biological brother of Jesus.
The move states Carrier's controlling evidentiary standard and neutralizes MacDonald's principal external attestation, leaving the historical hypothesis without the independence Carrier requires.
MacDonald's claim that mythologizing can surround real people and that Josephus independently identifies James as Jesus's biological brother.
Carrier concedes that real people may be mythologized, then argues that brother language could be cultic and that the Christ wording in Josephus was inserted later.
Paul's failure to cite the tax saying in Romans 13 indicates that Mark transformed Paul's tax teaching into the later coin story, illustrating gospel reification of Pauline material.
This concrete test case supports the mythicist literary-development mechanism and challenges the claim that gospel sayings preserve an independent historical Jesus tradition.
MacDonald's view that proposed derivation of Markan Jesus traditions from Paul is forced and that shared tradition better explains overlaps.
Carrier reasons that Paul would have cited an apt dominical tax saying had he known it, and therefore reads Mark's coin episode as a later narrative conversion.
Both historical-memory and literary-reification theories explain the tax evidence, and without evidence favoring either explanation they remain equally viable possibilities.
The methodological claim blocks MacDonald's appeal to plausibility from establishing historicity by requiring comparative evidence that differentiates the rival causal accounts.
MacDonald's criticism that Carrier's proposed alternative sources are unsupported speculation rather than historical evidence or argument.
Carrier responds that MacDonald likewise assumes derivation from Jesus, then frames the dispute as rival explanations requiring evidence that favors one over the other.
Assessments of historical probability must rest on contextual evidence that differentially supports one explanation over another.
This methodological claim establishes the evidential standard Carrier applies throughout his comparative case for a revelatory rather than historical Jesus.
MacDonald's distinction between interpretive evidence and comparative probability judgments.
After a boundary-spanning exchange about ambiguity and plausibility, Carrier argues that contextual evidence must support every differential probability assignment.
The temple-destruction saying reflects Pauline resurrection doctrine and does not independently indicate a historical failed prediction by Jesus.
The answer directly contests an asserted trajectory from an embarrassing historical saying to later spiritualization, a proposed indicator of an earthly Jesus.
The proposed historicist inference from Mark's failed temple prediction and John's later spiritual reinterpretation.
Carrier traces the saying through Paul and the Gospels, treating its variants as mythic reinterpretations of a tradition whose historical or revelatory origin remains unresolved.
Even an early expectation of a physical kingdom could derive from scriptural discovery or revelation rather than an earthly Jewish preacher.
The claim blocks another proposed inference from early apocalyptic content to a historical Jesus by supplying a specifically revelatory alternative source.
The suggestion that an originally physical kingdom expectation points to a failed historical Jewish preacher.
Following the moderator's kingdom-of-God hypothetical, Carrier says the primitive expectation, if established, could still originate in revelation or scriptural interpretation.
Q preserves both future-apocalyptic and presently operative conceptions of God's kingdom, which later Synoptic authors reposition for their own emphases.
The analysis offers a developmental textual model for kingdom traditions that can explain variation without reducing every early saying to a purely celestial revelation.
Carrier's claim that primitive kingdom expectations could originate with a revelatory Jesus or scriptural discovery.
MacDonald cites Q sayings about future arrival, present entry, John, mustard seed, and yeast, then explains later Synoptic variation as selective development of Q's ambiguity.
Early Christian theological formulations should be analyzed as changing social-identity markers that explain why sayings and missions were transformed.
The proposed social-identity framework supplies MacDonald's broader causal account of textual transformation across Jewish, Gentile, prewar, and postwar communities.
Moving beyond the kingdom example, MacDonald reframes theology as ideology and social identity, connecting textual changes to war, eschatology, ethnicity, and mission boundaries.
Social forces plausibly shape theology, but sparse and poor sources require evidential humility about reconstructing the earliest Christian developments.
Carrier accepts social explanation while limiting what historical reconstruction can establish, reinforcing the skeptical evidential constraint underlying his mythicist challenge.
MacDonald's proposal to reconstruct textual transformations through systematic social-identity analysis.
Carrier agrees that theology markets mundane social ideas and praises social-political reconstruction, while warning that biblical scholars often claim more certainty than the sources permit.
Paul's letters omit an earthly biography because no congregation disputed Jesus's humanity, while Paul's meetings with Cephas and James imply additional historical knowledge.
This is MacDonald's direct explanation of the Pauline silence that anchors Carrier's case, combining epistolary occasion with personal contact involving Jesus's brother.
The mythicist argument that Paul's failure to narrate Jesus's earthly ministry favors an originally revelatory Christ.
MacDonald argues that Paul wrote occasional letters rather than a Gospel, faced no denial of Jesus's humanity, and likely learned more about Jesus from Cephas and James than he recorded.
Second Peter, Ignatius, and First John indirectly attest Christians who denied the reality or historicity of Gospel narratives.
The claim directly rebuts MacDonald's assertion that early Christianity supplies no opposing voices and identifies surviving polemics as indirect evidence of such Christians.
MacDonald's claim that no early Christian opponents denied Jesus's humanity or his status as a Galilean teacher.
Carrier reads polemical assertions of eyewitness contact and condemnations of myths as evidence for otherwise-lost Christian factions that rejected the Gospel narratives' reality.
The mythicist argument from Paul concerns the expected incidental traces of an earthly life, not an explicit controversy over whether Jesus existed.
The distinction states the core Pauline-silence argument: many ordinary occasions should mention an earthly authority, yet Paul repeatedly locates knowledge of Jesus in revelation and scripture.
MacDonald's explanation that Paul's genre and undisputed assumptions gave him no reason to discuss a historical Jesus.

Carrier argues that an earthly teacher would generate questions, precedents, and biographical references throughout Paul's letters, whereas Paul repeatedly invokes revelation without comparable earthly placement.
Paul's silence is probabilistic evidence because the missing earthly references are less expected under historicity than under a revelatory-Christ hypothesis.
This move supplies the inferential warrant for treating Pauline silence as evidence and expressly identifies a probability disparity between historical and revelatory hypotheses.
MacDonald's objection that expecting earthly references from Paul is an unnecessary inference and an argument from silence.
Carrier argues that silence has evidential force when one hypothesis predicts missing material more strongly, contrasting Paul's lack of earthly biography with repeated revelatory references.
Josephus would not naturally understand a Christian title such as brother of the Lord as denoting a non-biological relationship.
The claim bears on whether the Josephus passage independently establishes that James was a biological sibling of Jesus.
The suggestion that Josephus normally uses brother language for literal biological relationships.
Carrier distinguishes Josephus's likely semantic understanding from the possibility that a Christian source used kinship language in a sectarian sense.
Josephus's ordinary treatment of brothers supports reading the James reference biologically because Josephus lacked knowledge of Pauline adoption doctrine.
This directly supports the historical-Jesus side's use of James as a biological relation and therefore as evidence of Jesus's existence.
Carrier's contention that Christian brother language may have been misunderstood or interpolated in Josephus.
MacDonald answers the semantic objection by appealing to Josephus's normal kinship usage and his presumed unfamiliarity with Christian adoptive-brother terminology.
Acts may preserve an early reading of Josephus in which James was understood as the brother of Jesus.
An early reception witness would strengthen the claim that Josephus's James passage originally referred to Jesus and was understood biologically.
Carrier's criticism that the Josephus wording and its underlying source cannot establish a biological brother of Jesus.
MacDonald invokes an argument associated with Steve Mason that Acts reflects knowledge of the Antiquities account and interpreted its James as Jesus's brother.
Acts neither recounts the same manner of James's death as Josephus nor identifies its James as the brother of Jesus.
The objections undermine Acts as an early corroborating witness for MacDonald's biological identification of James in Josephus.
MacDonald's claim that Acts supplies an early reader who understood Josephus to mean Jesus's brother.
Carrier separates the Acts and Josephus narratives by emphasizing their different death accounts and the absence of an explicit fraternal identification in Acts.
Josephus's narrative most naturally concerns a Christian James whose Torah stance provoked a harsh Sadducean response, making Carrier's alternative identification forced.
This is MacDonald's principal contextual argument that the James episode fits Jesus's followers and favors the historical identification despite textual uncertainty.
Carrier's objections that Acts does not identify James and that Josephus may not refer to Jesus Christ at all.
MacDonald combines the contrast between harsh and tolerant Torah interpretation, the narrative ordering of names, and the lack of another known Jesus with a brother James.
The James passage can coherently refer to Jesus ben Damneus, while its wording and procedural context do not establish a Christian James or persecution over Torah interpretation.
This supplies the mythicist side's main alternative explanation of Josephus and directly contests one of the strongest proposed extra-biblical historicity arguments.
MacDonald's claim that Josephus's naming pattern, Torah conflict, and narrative probabilities identify James as Jesus's brother.
Carrier argues that delayed patronymics occur in Josephus, proposes scribal displacement involving Jesus ben Damneus, and interprets the complaint as opposition to an unlawfully convened court.
Josephus contrasts harsh Sadducean legal interpretation with a more accurate and tolerant approach, implying substantive Torah conflict beyond a merely procedural complaint.
The interpretation reconnects the James episode to a distinctive religious dispute and resists Carrier's attempt to reduce it to court procedure.
Carrier's reading that the citizens objected only to an illegally assembled Sanhedrin rather than the treatment of James.
MacDonald treats the procedural appeal as one component of a broader clash between strict temple-protective Sadducees and people favoring more tolerant Torah observance.
The passage describes Ananus as brutal and the Sadducees as rigid, but locates the citizens' actual objection in his breach of lawful procedure.
This preserves Carrier's non-Christian procedural reading of Josephus against MacDonald's attempt to infer a conflict over competing Torah interpretations.
MacDonald's argument that the vocabulary reveals two competing approaches to Torah and concern for James's religious group.
Carrier distinguishes character descriptions from the stated ground of protest, maintaining that the citizens objected to Ananus acting unlawfully rather than enforcing Torah too severely.
Carrier counts the brother-of-the-Lord material as evidence for historicity, yet judges the total case to leave only about a one-in-three chance that Jesus existed.
The statement summarizes Carrier's calibrated bottom-line position on the debate motion while clarifying that he does not simply discard contrary evidence.
The host's suggestion that brother-of-the-Lord evidence might support a historical Jesus despite Carrier's interpretation.
Carrier explains that his probabilistic case already credits the James material toward historicity and also regards a theory like MacDonald's as plausible conditional on existence.
The evidence strongly favors a historical Jesus who was mythologized very early, although the gospel authors' adaptations make the underlying historical person difficult to recover.
This is MacDonald's direct bottom-line resolution of the motion and explains how historicity remains compatible with extensive early mythologization.
Carrier's roughly one-in-three historicity estimate and the moderator's request for MacDonald's corresponding probability.
MacDonald gives historicity a much higher probability while retaining scholarly uncertainty, then stresses that well-meaning gospel reshaping obscures recoverable historical details.
